title: Samsung Galaxy Watch 9, Ultra 2 Expected July 22 Unpacked
excerpt: Samsung confirmed Galaxy Unpacked for July 22, where the Galaxy Watch 9 and Ultra 2 are expected. Here's whether to buy a Watch now or wait.
body:
Samsung has locked in July 22 for its next Galaxy Unpacked, and two new smartwatches are expected to headline it: the Galaxy Watch 9 and the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2. If you've been about to buy a Galaxy Watch, that date is your cue to stop and hold the wallet for 48 hours.

## What's Coming at Samsung's July 22 Unpacked

Samsung officially confirmed the event. Galaxy Unpacked streams live from London on July 22 at 9 a.m. ET. The company hasn't named the watches on the invite, but the leak trail is consistent enough that the lineup is close to a given. New foldables are expected to share the stage, though the wearables are the part that matters if you're shopping in the sub-$700 smartwatch range.

Here's what the reporting points to. The Galaxy Watch 9 is said to start around $349, adding ultra-wideband for precise device tracking, a new heart health score, and hearing monitoring. Leakers put the 40mm model's battery near 400mAh, a sizable jump over the Watch 8 in the same case size. The step-up Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is reported at $699, with an 800mAh battery (roughly 35 percent larger than the first Ultra), a brighter 3,000-nit display, and three experimental health sensors that track advanced glycation end-products, antioxidant levels, and vascular load. Both are expected to run One UI 9 Watch on Wear OS 7, and the Ultra 2 would be the debut device for Qualcomm's 3nm Snapdragon Wear Elite chip, a partnership Samsung put on record earlier this year.

Treat the prices and specs as leaks until Samsung says the words on stage. The date is the confirmed part. Pre-orders are expected to open the same day, with retail availability reported for August 5.

## What It Means for Buyers

Two things happen the moment a new Galaxy Watch launches. The obvious one: a newer watch with a bigger battery and fresh sensors arrives. The one buyers forget: the previous generations get cheaper, often fast. If the Watch 9 lands at $349, expect the outgoing models to slide on Amazon and at Samsung directly within days.

That matters because the older Galaxy Watch is already a strong buy. In [our Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 review](/posts/samsung-galaxy-watch-7-review-flagship-smarts-under-200) we called it flagship smarts for under $200, and a launch like this is exactly the kind of event that pushes that sort of deal lower still. The new health sensors on the Ultra 2 are the genuine unknown. AGEs and vascular-load tracking aren't features you'll find on any wrist today, and until independent reviewers see how accurate they are, nobody should pay $699 on the promise alone.

Who should care about the new watches? People who want the biggest battery and the newest chip, plus Ultra buyers who like the rugged titanium case. Who should ignore the hype? Anyone who mainly wants notifications, workouts, and sleep tracking. That job is already handled well by watches that are about to get a price cut.

## Buy or Wait?

Wait. Even if you have zero interest in the Watch 9 or the Ultra 2, the July 22 event is worth two days of patience. New models almost always drag down the prices of last year's watches, so holding off either lands you the newer hardware or a cheaper older one. There's no version of buying on July 21 that comes out ahead.

If you're set on the latest, watch the pre-orders that open on the 22nd. Samsung usually bundles trade-in credit and a free band or a storage upgrade in that first window, which is where the real savings on a new watch tend to hide. If you just want a great smartwatch for the least money, let the launch happen, then check the tracked price on last year's model. That's the moment the value shows up.

title: Anker SOLIX C300 Review: Is This Power Station Worth It?
excerpt: The Anker SOLIX C300 packs 288Wh and three AC outlets for about $209. Here's who it's for, what it can't run, and when to actually buy.
body:
Every summer it plays out the same way. A storm knocks the power out for six hours, your phone slides to 4 percent, and the milk in the fridge starts its slow march toward the trash. A 288Wh battery like the Anker SOLIX C300 won't run your whole house, but it will keep phones, a laptop, a CPAP machine, and a few lights alive long enough to ride out the outage. The real question is whether this specific unit, at around $209, is the one to buy.

---

## What Is the Anker SOLIX C300?

The Anker SOLIX C300 is a 288Wh portable power station: a battery in a box with a handle, built to charge your gear when there's no wall outlet nearby. It runs on LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) cells, the same chemistry Anker rates for 3,000 full charge cycles before capacity drops to 80 percent. Drain it flat and refill it every single day, and you're looking at roughly eight years before it noticeably weakens.

It pushes 300W continuous (600W surge) across eight ports: three AC outlets, a car socket, two 140W USB-C ports, a smaller 15W USB-C, and a USB-A. That 140W USB-C matters more than the AC outlets for most people, because it fast-charges a MacBook Pro or a Steam Deck directly, no power brick required. The whole thing weighs about eight pounds, so it's a two-finger carry from the trunk to the campsite, not a piece of furniture.

---

## Who Should Buy the Anker SOLIX C300?

This is a weekend-and-emergency battery, and knowing that upfront saves you from disappointment. Buy the C300 if you camp, road-trip, or tailgate and want to keep phones, a drone, a camera, and a laptop topped up for a couple of days off-grid. Buy it if you want an outage cushion that keeps the essentials going: a router, a few LED lights, phones, and a CPAP through the night.

Skip it if you're shopping for real home backup. 288Wh is under a third of a kilowatt-hour, which won't carry a refrigerator far, and the 300W ceiling rules out anything with a heating element. If whole-home is the goal, you want a 1,000Wh-plus unit and a much bigger budget. The C300 is the everyday, throw-it-in-the-car size, and it's honest about that.

---

## What the Anker SOLIX C300 Gets Right

- **Three real AC outlets, not just USB.** Plenty of 300W-class batteries skimp here. The C300 gives you full wall sockets for a laptop charger, a fan, or a string of lights, so you're not hunting for adapters.
- **140W USB-C both directions.** The main USB-C port fills a modern laptop at full speed and refills the C300 itself the same way, so one PD 3.1 cable does double duty.
- **Fast top-ups.** From a wall outlet, Anker and verified owners both put it at roughly 0 to 80 percent in under an hour. You can pull it off the shelf, splash-charge it the morning of a trip, and go.
- **LiFePO4 longevity.** That 3,000-cycle rating outlasts older lithium-ion power stations by years, and the cells hold a charge for months in storage.
- **Genuinely quiet.** Verified-purchase owners consistently report the fan rarely spins for small loads, and professional reviewers put it around 25 to 30dB under heavier AC draw. It won't wake a tent.

---

## What You'll Pay

The C300 launched at a $299 list price and spends most of its life below it. As of this writing it sits around $209, and mid-July 2026 deal coverage from Gizmodo and Kotaku flagged it slipping toward an all-time low near $199. That's the pattern to watch: this isn't a product you pay full MSRP for. The price widget above this article shows where today's number lands against the history we track, so you can tell at a glance whether $209 is a genuine low or just an average week. For a 288Wh LiFePO4 unit with three AC outlets and a 140W USB-C port, anything in the low $200s is fair, and sub-$200 is the moment to grab it.

---

## The Anker SOLIX C300 vs. the Alternatives

If you only ever charge phones, laptops, and cameras and never need a wall outlet, a big USB power bank like the one in our [Anker 737 Power Bank review](/posts/anker-737-power-bank-work-from-anywhere) is smaller, cheaper, and pocket-friendly, though it holds far less than the C300. The EcoFlow River 3 is the closest direct rival at a similar size and price, and it's the better pick if you want a faster AC recharge and don't mind EcoFlow's app. The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus deserves a look if you're already in Jackery's solar ecosystem, but it usually charges over USB-C slower than the C300's 140W port.

---

## One Thing to Consider Before Buying

The 300W output ceiling is the real limit, and it catches people off guard. Three AC outlets sound generous until you realize the combined draw can't cross 300W continuous. No microwave, no hair dryer, no space heater, no coffee maker, no full-size electric kettle. Those pull 700W to 1,500W and trip the inverter the instant you plug them in. The C300 is for electronics and low-wattage gear, full stop. There's also lineup confusion to sidestep: the C300, the DC-only C300 DC, and the newer C300X share a name but differ on outlets and price, so check the exact listing before you click buy.

---

## Anker SOLIX C300 FAQ

**Q: Can the Anker SOLIX C300 run a full-size refrigerator?**
Not for long, and probably not at all. A typical fridge surges well past the 300W inverter limit the moment its compressor kicks in. The C300 is built for phones, laptops, routers, lights, fans, and a CPAP, not major appliances.

**Q: How many times can it charge a phone?**
With 288Wh of capacity, most owners get roughly 15 to 25 full smartphone charges depending on the phone, or a couple of full laptop refills. That's enough to keep a small group's devices alive through a long weekend.

**Q: Is the C300 worth it over a cheaper USB power bank?**
If you need AC outlets or want to power something for a full day, yes. If you only charge USB devices, a large power bank costs less and fits in a bag. The C300 earns its price the moment you need wall outlets off-grid or a cushion during an outage.

---

## The Verdict

The Anker SOLIX C300 is the right size of portable power for camping trips and short outages, with battery longevity and quiet, fast charging that punch above its price. Buy it when the price dips into the low $200s or below, and don't expect it to run anything with a heating element.

---

If the current price in the card above sits near $200 or under, this is an easy yes for a first power station. If it's back at the $299 list, wait a week for the next dip.
